title: The five-second favour: small help, offered early
description: Most kindness costs almost nothing because it is offered early: the held door before the struggle, the offered seat before the wobble. Why timing, not size, is what makes small help feel large.

body.heading: Help has a timing curve
paragraphs: The same act is worth very different amounts depending on when it arrives. A hand offered while someone is still gathering their bags feels like attentiveness; the identical hand offered after they have dropped everything feels like rescue — welcome, but it confirms they were struggling. Early help protects dignity as well as arms.

This is why small favours punch above their weight. Five seconds of noticing — holding the lift, offering the seat, picking up the dropped glove and returning it — tells the other person they are seen, which is most of what kindness ever communicates.

body.heading: Make noticing a habit, not a mood
paragraphs: You cannot schedule generosity, but you can schedule attention. The practical trick is a trigger: every time you go through a door, look behind you; every time you sit on a bus, scan once for who is standing. Attach the look to something you already do and the favours start finding you.
None of this requires being an especially good person. It requires being a slightly earlier one — and earlier, most days, is entirely within reach.

takeaway: Small help offered early is worth more than the same help offered late: it protects dignity, signals that someone is noticed, and costs about five seconds.
